issues.body_excerpt:
### Problem Description

The documentation for `pandas.read_csv(usecols=[...])` says that it treats the iterable list of columns like an unordered set (updated in https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/18673 and #53763), so the returned dataframe won't necessarily have the same column order. This is different behaviour from other pandas data reading methods (e.g., `pandas.read_parquet(columns=[...])`). I think the order should be preserved. ### Problem Description

Users should be able to accessing a dataframe element–that is an Arrow-backed map–with normal python dict semantics.

Today, accessing an *Arrow-backed* map element will return a list of tuples per [`as_py()`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/3832e85779b143d882ce501c24ee51df95799e2c/pandas/core/arrays/arrow/array.py#L639) from [`MapScalar`](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/python/generated/pyarrow.MapScalar.html) type–thus list semantics and not dictionary access semantics. Historically, this is because Arrow allows multiple keys, and ordering is not enforced. So converting to a python dictionary removes those two behaviors. issues.title: DOC: Series.name is just Hashable, but many column arguments require str
issues.body_excerpt:
### Location of the documentation

* https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/reference/api/pandas.Series.name.html
* https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.pivot.html

### Documentation problem

In the documentation, `Series.name` is [just required to be](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/reference/api/pandas.Series.name.html) a `Hashable`. When `pandas` functions ask for a column label, however, it often asks for an `str`, e.g. in [DataFrame.pivot](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.pivot.html), where it says
> **columns**: *str or object or a list of str*

### Suggested fix for documentation

Use `Hashable` everywhere to column labels as a function argument

issues.title: Use BaseExecutionEngine for Python and Numba engines
issues.body_excerpt:
In #61032 we have created a new base class `BaseExecutionEngine` that engines can subclass to handle `apply` and `map` operations. The base class has been initially created to allow third-party engines to be passed to `DataFrame.apply(..., engine=third_party_engine)`. But our core engines Python and Numba can also be implemented as instances of this base class. This will make the code cleaner, more maintainable, and it may allow to move the Numba engine outside of the pandas code base easily.

The whole migration to the new interface is quite a big change, so it's recommended to make the transition step by step, in small pull requests.

issues.title: CI: Micromamba taking too long to resolve the environments in the CI
issues.body_excerpt:
Our CI jobs are frequently failing now as they timeout after 90 minutes of execution. Of those 90 minutes, 25 are spent on micromamba resolving the environment.

In the past we have fixed this by limiting the number of packages to be considered. For example, if the environment just says `numpy`, maybe there are 200 versions that will be considered. While if we say `numpy >= 2` the number can be limited to few.

I'm not sure which packages have lots of options, and we don't want to filter out the versions that make sense to install. But we should have a look and see if by adding few constraints we can get a reasonable time to solve the environment.

OpenPyXL/Xlrd Engine + Format Detection

In [PDEP-9](https://pandas.pydata.org/pdeps/0009-io-extensions.html) it was discussed the possibility of allowing third-party packages to automatically add `pandas.read_<format>` functions and `DataFrame.to_<format>` methods. This is less ambitious, since it doesn't allow adding new formats to pandas (e.g. `pandas.read_dicom`, a format for medical data), but it still have the rest of the advantages of PDEP-9:

issues.title: Unpin Python version in the development environment
issues.body_excerpt:
xref #61555

Our base conda environment `environment.yml` is used locally by pandas developers (contributors and maintainers), and for some CI jobs, like building the documentation. For stability, we pinned the version of Python to a specific version (currently `python=3.10`). As new versions of Python are released, this is becoming outdated, and for no particular reason we're now going building our docs and creating our development environments in a Python version soon to stop being supported.

This issue is to remove the pin, leave `python` open to any version, which in general it should be the latest available, and fix all the problems in the CI caused by upgrading the version here.

The errors detected when upgrading can be found here:

issues.title: BUG: `explode()` converts timestamps at millisecond resolution in DatetimeIndex to nanosecond resolution
issues.body_excerpt:
### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
test = pd.Series([pd.date_range("2020-01-01T00:00:00Z", "2020-01-01T02:00:00Z", freq="1h", unit="ms")])
test.explode().dtype
```

### Issue Description

The docs for `pd.date_range` state that the `unit` keyword argument is the resolution of timestamps in the returned DatetimeIndex, which is true---and counter to the usage of `unit` elsewhere, e.g. in `pd.to_datetime`. Regardless of this discrepancy, `explode` does not respect the millisecond resolution of timestamps in a DatetimeIndex, converting them to nanosecond resolution in the returned Series or DataFrame.

### Expected Behavior

dtypes should not be changed by `explode`.

issues.body_excerpt:
### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

arr = np.array([-1j, 0j, 1j], dtype=complex)

print(s.var(ddof=0))  # -0.666
```

### Issue Description

1. The results diverge from numpy.
2. pandas yields nonsensical results like negative floats.

### Expected Behavior

For complex variables, `std` and `var` should give non-negative floating results. Recall that $` σ ≔ \sqrt{𝔼|x-μ|^2 } `$. Often, authors that only use real-valued variables leave out the absolute value, which I guess is what happened here.

issues.title: Proposal: Add pd.check(df) utility function for quick dataset diagnostics
issues.body_excerpt:
### Problem Description

While working with pandas DataFrames during exploratory data analysis (EDA), analysts frequently perform the same manual steps to understand their dataset:

- Count null and non-null values
- Check unique value counts
- Estimate missing percentages

These operations are often repeated multiple times, especially after data cleaning, filtering, or merging. Currently, users rely on combinations like:
```
df.isnull().sum()
df.nunique()
df.notnull().sum()
```
There is no single built-in pandas utility that offers this all-in-one diagnostic view.

### Feature Description

Add a utility function pd.check(df) that returns a concise column-wise summary of a DataFrame’s structure, including:

- Unique values per column
- Non-null value counts
- Missing value counts
- Missing

issues.title: ENH: Add `excel_sep_hint` parameter to `to_csv` for Excel compatibility
issues.body_excerpt:
### Problem Description
It would be great if Pandas could generate CSV files that Excel automatically opens with the correct delimiter. When using semicolons or other non-comma separators, Excel often opens CSV files with all data in one column unless a `sep=` hint is present at the beginning of the file. Currently, users must write custom code to add this hint.


### Feature Description
Add a boolean parameter `excel_sep_hint` to `to_csv()` that prepends a delimiter hint for Excel:

```python
def to_csv(self, ..., excel_sep_hint=False):
    """
    excel_sep_hint : bool, default False
        If True, prepend 'sep=' line to help Excel detect delimiter
    """
```

Usage:
```python
df.to_csv('data.csv', sep=';', excel_sep_hint=True)
```

Output:
```
sep=;
col1;col2;col3
val1;val2;val3
```

issues.title: PERF: Arrow dtypes are much slower than Numpy for DataFrame.apply
issues.body_excerpt:
The same code with `DataFrame.apply` is >4x slower when the data is in Arrow dtypes versus Numpy.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import pyarrow as pa
import time

NUM_ROWS = 500_000
df = pd.DataFrame({"A": np.arange(NUM_ROWS) % 30, "B": np.arange(NUM_ROWS)+1.0})
print(df.dtypes)
df2 = df.astype({"A": pd.ArrowDtype(pa.int64()), "B": pd.ArrowDtype(pa.float64())})
print(df2.dtypes)

t0 = time.time()
df.apply(lambda r: 0 if r.A == 0 else (r.B // r.A), axis=1)
print(f"Non-Arrow time: {time.time() - t0:.2f} seconds")

t0 = time.time()
df2.apply(lambda r: 0 if r.A == 0 else (r.B // r.A), axis=1)
print(f"Arrow time: {time.time() - t0:.2f} seconds")
```

### Location of the documentation

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/io/html.py


### Documentation problem

Several functions in `pandas/io/html.py` have docstrings that violate [PEP 257](https://peps.python.org/pep-0257/) and pandas documentation guidelines. Flagged violations include:

- `D400`: Docstring summary should end with a period

When parsing CSVs with `pd.read_csv`, there is no function‑scoped way to (a) react to malformed rows as they happen and (b) capture the exact CSV line numbers for those rows, without introducing process‑global side effects or using a subprocess.

issues.title: DEPR: rename 'unit' keyword in to_datetime etc
issues.body_excerpt:
to_datetime, to_timedelta, Timestamp, and Timedelta have a `unit` keyword that causes confusion because the term 'unit' is overloaded.  The keyword refers to how we interpret integer arguments, while the result's obj.unit attribute refers to the resolution of the result.  Confusion e.g. #60371.

Update: also the meaning of the keyword in date_range matches the attribute but not the to_datetime meaning.

Let's deprecate the argument and rename it to something else.  Opening bid: "numeric_unit"

Quick troubleshooting tips for common build/install issues

This combination of pandas and python version is used by the Databricks Runtime [16.4](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/release-notes/runtime/16.4lts) (current LTS). When testing code meant for this runtime in a CI/CD environment, pandas needs to be built from source or cached somewhere. Building pandas from source regularly is cumbersome, as is setting up a custom cache for this. Is it possible to release a wheel of that version for python 3.12?

issues.title: BUG: `record_prefix` ignored when `record_path` is empty
issues.body_excerpt:
### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

_s = pd.Series([    {"k": f"{i}", "m": "q"} for i in range(5)
])

pd.json_normalize(_s,record_prefix="T")
```

### Issue Description

The `record_prefix` is completely ignored and the resulting columns are note renamed.

```
   k  m
0  0  q
1  1  q
2  2  q
3  3  q
4  4  q
```

The issue is in [L517-L527](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/io/json/_normalize.py#L517-L527) where a short cut is taken for speed.
One option to fix this would be to pass the `record_prefix` as `prefix` to `nested_to_record`.

This is hidden in the documentation example by using a positional argument for the record path

```
    >>> data = {"A": [1, 2]}
    >>> pd.json_normalize(data, "A", record_prefix="Prefix.")
        Prefix.0
    0

issues.title: API: `freq` or `step` for base class Index?
issues.body_excerpt:
Brainstorming, not advocating:

Thinking about #60561 about how to make `Index[timestamp[pyarrow]]` either _be_ a DatetimeIndex or behave like one, one approach is to take DTI methods and move their logic to the base class behind a `self.dtype.kind == "M"` check.  This almost works, but some of those methods check for `self.freq` which the base class doesn't have.

But `freq` for DTI/TDI means basically the same thing as `step` does for `RangeIndex`.  And `step` could be well-defined for any dtype where subtraction is defined.

What if we defined `step` on the base class, had it be an alias for freq on DTI/TDI?  Could get rid of a ton of special-casing in the DTI/TDI classes.  When it is present, it would enable some optimizations (e.g. we know we are monotonic, can fastpath some setops).

You are setting values through chained assignment. A typical example is when you are setting values in a column of a DataFrame, like:

issues.title: DOC: Replace `@Appender`, `@Substitution`, `@doc` with inlined docstrings
issues.body_excerpt:
Since pandas has objects with the same API, e.g. `DataFrame.fillna` `Series.fillna`, some of these methods may leverage a shared docstring system using `@Appender`, `@Substitution`, `@doc` and variables named like `shared_docs`to dynamically generate docstring based on a template. While this helps reduce some duplication, the downsides are:

1. The shared docstring system, at minimum, adds indirection and, at worse, is less clear than a hardcoded docstring for new contributions
2. Since these docstrings are dynamic, they avoid docstring standardization and rules provide by Ruff. (These docstrings are validated by flake8 run in a subprocess, but it would be nice to remove this https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/98c9c7f838d223e66f1459fab23ac178b29c2227/scripts/validate_docstrings.py#L

issues.title: ENH: Migrate from ujson to orjson
issues.body_excerpt:
Ref: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/62072

issues.title: Remove take action from CI
issues.body_excerpt:
The take action in github is well intentioned, but may be causing more harm than good. Often users comment "take" but progress immediately stalls, and new contributors can be discouraged from pursuing issues that are already assigned to users.

As an alternative, we can document better expectations for "soft reserving" an issue, much like sci-kit learn has done in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/31568

issues.title: BUG: `pandas.date_range()` raises `NonExistentTimeError` despite `nonexistent="shift_forward"` when crossing DST boundaries
issues.body_excerpt:
### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

start = pd.Timestamp("2024-04-26 01:00:00", tz="Africa/Cairo")
end = pd.Timestamp("2024-04-27 00:00:00", tz="Africa/Cairo")
tz = "Africa/Cairo"
freq = "D"

full_range = pd.date_range(
    start=start,
    end=end,
    freq=freq,
    tz=tz,
    nonexistent="shift_forward",  # should handle DST spring forward
    ambiguous=True,               # should handle DST fall back
    normalize=True,
)
```

### Issue Description

`pandas.date_range()` raises `NonExistentTimeError` when the generated range crosses a daylight saving time (DST) transition,  
even when the user explicitly provides `nonexistent="shift_forward"` and `ambiguous=True`.

This makes it impossible to safely generate timezone-aware ranges that include DST boundaries.

issues.title: ENH: Prevent filling in `unstack()`
issues.body_excerpt:
### Problem Description

It's pretty common when using `DataFrame.unstack()` that the `fill_value` argument does not need to be used because there is a 1:1 mapping of the cells in the stacked and unstacked tables. This is the case when the dataframe/series was produced with `stack()`.

Oftentimes this is the expectation and if any filling does occur it represents a problem in the data. It would be good if this assumption could be made explicit with an argument that causes an exception to be raised if it is violated.

### Feature Description

Add a new Boolean keyword argument named `nofill` or similar to `DataFrame.unstack()` and `Series.unstack()`. The default value should be False. If True and the value for any cell is missing, raise a `ValueError` instead of substituting the fill value.

issues.title: fillna for np.float64(np.nan)

I like `pd.Float64Dtype()` and other pandas datatypes, but one small glitch found in below minimal case:

```python
import pandas as pd

print((df['b'] / df['a']).fillna(0))
# 0    0.5
# 1    NaN
# 2    0.0
# dtype: Float64

# np.float64(nan)
```

Is there any plan to make `fillna` adapt to `np.float64(np.nan)`? Or make sure `0 / 0` in `pd.Float64Dtype()` can return `pd.NA` rather than `np.float64(np.nan)`?

issues.title: BUG: Index.intersection returns reference instead of new instance
issues.body_excerpt:
### Reproducible Example

```python
>>> import pandas as pd
>>>
>>> index1 = pd.Index([0, 1])
>>> index2 = pd.Index([0, 1])

True
```

### Issue Description

The [documentation](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Index.intersection.html) for `Index.intersection` states:
> This returns a new Index with elements common to the index and other.

However, there are cases where a reference to one of the operands is returned instead of a new instance.  Subsequent operations on the returned object can end up mutating one of the operands, which is unexpected.

### Expected Behavior

`Index.intersection` should always return a new instance.

issues.title: PDEP-8 inplace keyword deprecation - implementation tracker issue
issues.body_excerpt:
Issue to track the progress of implementing the accepted PDEP-8: https://pandas.pydata.org/pdeps/0008-inplace-methods-in-pandas.html

Summary of the PDEP proposed changes:

- The ``inplace`` parameter will be removed from any method which can never update the
  underlying values of a pandas object inplace or which alters the shape of the object,
  and where the `inplace=True` option is only syntactic sugar for reassigning the result
  to the calling DataFrame/Series.
  - In practice, this are the methods `drop`, `rename`, `rename_axis`, ``reset_index``,  ``set_index``, `dropna` `drop_duplicates`, `sort_values`, `sort_index`, `eval`, `query`
- The `inplace` parameter is kept for those methods that can
  modify the underlying values of a pandas object inplace, such as `fillna` or `replace`,

issues.title: BUG: Inconsistent behavior with groupby and copy-on-write
issues.body_excerpt:
Grouping by a Series and the mutating that Series can have different impacts whether a view on the data exists.

```python
ser = pd.Series([1, 2, 1])
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6]})
gb = df.groupby(ser)
ser.iloc[0] = 100
print(gb.sum())
#      a  b
# 1    3  6
# 2    2  5
# 100  1  4

ser = pd.Series([1, 2, 1])
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6]})
ser2 = ser[:]
gb = df.groupby(ser)
ser.iloc[0] = 100
print(gb.sum())
#    a   b
# 1  4  10
# 2  2   5
```

This only happens for certain paths in groupby, e.g. using

    ser = pd.Series(pd.Categorical([1, 2, 1], categories=[1, 2, 100]))

gives the latter behavior. We should be taking a shallow copy of any grouping Series when we create the `DataFrameGroupBy` instance.

issues.title: Constructor with invalid unicode: automatically fall back to object dtype?
issues.body_excerpt:
We documented that invalid unicode can no longer be stored in a `str` dtype column (https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/user_guide/migration-3-strings.html#invalid-unicode-input), and for sure that will error when you explicitly ask for `str`:

```python
>>> pd.Series(['\ud800'], dtype=str)
...
UnicodeEncodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't encode character '\ud800' in position 0: surrogates not allowed
```

But I am wondering if we should still by default fall back to object dtype in the case you are not specifying a dtype, i.e. for the default inference. Right now also `pd.Series(['\ud800'])` gives the same error. 
(it might be a performance cost in validating that up front though, or otherwise we could the specific error if we know we started without user-specified dtype)

issues.title: DEP: Drop NumPy 1.26 support
issues.body_excerpt:
Discussed in the community meeting today. While NumPy 1.26 is EOL according to Spec0, and SciPy has dropped it from main, they won't be releasing for a bit longer. rgommers has mentioned:

https://github.com/scientific-python/specs/issues/386#issuecomment-3619804433

> The recommendation is definitely the right thing to do, so I'd say don't drop NumPy 1.26 support until mid 2026. SPEC 0 is already very agressive, and any gaps in a regular release schedule or something out of the ordinary like an ABI break exacerbate that (and numpy 2.0 has both of those, it was also 6 months late).

I believe the way forward is to keep 1.26 in pandas 3.0, and look to drop it at the appropriate time in pandas 3.1 or 3.2 depending on when those get released.

cc jorisvandenbossche mroeschke jbrockmendel

issues.title: ENH: Add read/write support for the Vortex columnar format
issues.body_excerpt:
### Problem Description

Pandas currently has no way to read or write data in the Vortex format (https://lf-ai.github.io/vortex/), a new open columnar storage format developed under the Linux Foundation. As Vortex adoption grows, pandas users cannot easily load these datasets without first converting them to Parquet or Arrow, adding unnecessary steps and limiting interoperability.

### Feature Description

Add optional pandas IO support for Vortex, similar to existing Parquet and Arrow readers/writers. This could include:

- `pd.read_vortex(path, **kwargs)`
- `DataFrame.to_vortex(path, **kwargs)`

Support may rely on a Python Vortex library or an Arrow-based bridge if one becomes available.

### Alternative Solutions

- Convert Vortex → Parquet or Arrow → pandas
- Use custom Python wrapper

issues.title: String dtype: differences in regex operations because of engine (Python vs RE2)
issues.body_excerpt:
One area where there can be significant behaviour differences depending on the string dtype backend being used (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/63105) is for regex operations:

- The Python str object-dtype based implementation uses the Python stdlib `re` module, which I think was generally based on the PCRE engine but has diverged from it.
- On the other hand, for the pyarrow-backed string dtype, the Arrow C++ / pyarrow library uses the [RE2](https://github.com/google/re2) engine.

And unfortunately, there are lots of different regular expression engines with slight differences in behaviour and supported features (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparison_of_regular_expression_engines).

We already encountered a few differences: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/60833

issues.body_excerpt:
Pandas Version Checks

 I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
 I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of pandas.
 I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.


Issue Description
The PyArrow string backend uses the RE2 regex engine, which does not support backreferences (e.g., \1, \2, \3). Currently, using str.contains() and other string methods with backreference patterns raises a raw pyarrow.lib.ArrowInvalid error.
This is related to but distinct from issue #60833 (lookarounds) and PR #63613, which handle lookaround assertions. Backreferences are a separate regex feature that also fails with RE2.
As PyArrow becomes the default backend in pandas 3.0, this will cause regressions for users relying on backreferences in regex

issues.title: BUG: `DataFrame.from_records` ignores exclude argument when `nrows=0`
issues.body_excerpt:
### Reproducible Example

```python
from pandas import DataFrame
# Create sample data
rows = [
    {"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3},
    {"a": 4, "b": 5, "c": 6},
    {"a": 7, "b": 8, "c": 9},
]

result = DataFrame.from_records(
           iter(rows), columns=["a", "b", "c"], exclude = ["b"], nrows=0
       )

assert (result.columns == ["a", "c"]).all(), "Column exclusion did not work as expected"
```

### Issue Description

In Pandas 2.3.3, `result.columns` was empty when `nrows=0`. This issue was reported in Issue #61140 and fixed in #62085. However, this PR seem to accidentally cause regression in which DataFrame.from_records ignored `exclude` argument. In Pandas 3.0.0rc2, result.columns will be ["a", "b", "c"] and do not exclude ["b"]

### Expected Behavior

result.columns should be ["a", "c"]

Aggregations are using `check_result_array` to verify that the aggregation operation reduced the dimension. issues.body_excerpt:
ATM Period subtraction gives an Offset object.  Subtraction with PeriodDtype array gives an object dtype array of Offsets:

```
per1 = pd.Period("2016-01-01", "M")
per2 = pd.Period("2017-01-01", "M")

left = pd.Series([per1])
right = pd.Series([per2])

>>> left - right
0    <-12 * MonthEnds>
dtype: object
```

A better result in this example would be a `timedelta64[M]` dtype.  There are two problems with this:

  c) "Y-JAN", "Y-FEB", ... for which "Y" is the timedelta64 unit.

issues.title: DEPR: Period "freq" -> "unit"
issues.body_excerpt:
Discussed in last week's meeting and before that in #61897, but before pulling the trigger on the rest of this (#64155 and more) I decided to write up The Whole Thing:

### Motivation

There are 2 longstanding issues with the Period/PeriodDtype/PeriodArray/PeriodIndex API I'd like to address:

1) "freq" means something different in the Period context than it does for DatetimeIndex/TimedeltaIndex (xref #47227)

2) Period.freq being a DateOffset makes users incorrectly expect that *all* DateOffsets have associated Periods (xref #5091, #12379, etc)

To fix this, I propose to change (with deprecation cycle) the Period classes to use "unit" instead of "freq", with unit being a string analogous to Timestamp.unit/DatetimeIndex.unit.  This will include:

- The `freq` keyword in Period, PeriodIndex

issues.title: API: PeriodIndex(dt64_data) depends on container for data
issues.body_excerpt:
```
data = np.arange(5).view("M8[D]").astype("M8[ns]")
dti = pd.DatetimeIndex(data)
assert dti.freq is None

pd.PeriodIndex(dti)             # <- raises bc no freq
pd.PeriodIndex(pd.Series(dti))  # <- infers freq="D" 
```

PeriodIndex goes through period_array -> PeriodArray._from_datetime64 -> dt64arr_to_periodarr.  When no freq is specified, this does

```
    if freq is None:
        if isinstance(data, ABCIndex):
            data, freq = data._values, data.freq
        elif isinstance(data, ABCSeries):
            data, freq = data._values, data.dt.freq
```

In the Series case we get `data.dt.freq`, which uses `inferred_freq` instead of `freq` (which is always `None` inside a Series).

I think we should consider this inconsistency a bug and always use data._values.freq.

issues.body_excerpt:
### Reproducible Example

## Issue

In `pandas/io/stata.py` line 285, the `parse_dates_safe` function uses `Series.apply` with a lambda to extract year and month from object-dtype datetime columns:

```python
year_month = dates.apply(lambda x: 100 * x.year + x.month)
d["year"] = year_month._values // 100
d["month"] = year_month._values - d["year"] * 100
```
This iterates element-by-element through Python, which is slow for large DataFrames. The sibling datetime64 branch already uses vectorized DatetimeIndex operations for the same task (lines 258-261).

## Proposed Fix
Replace with:

```python
date_index = DatetimeIndex(dates)
d["year"] = date_index._data.year
d["month"] = date_index._data.month
```

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

df = pd.DataFrame({"A": [1, 2, 3], "B": [4, 5, 6]})
ser = pd.Series(pd.array([7, pd.NA, 9]))
mask = np.ones(df.shape, dtype=bool)

`Index.take` has two bugs when `allow_fill=True` and `fill_value` is passed explicitly:

### 1. `fill_value` is silently discarded

The caller's `fill_value` is ignored; `self._na_value` is always substituted:

```python

When a DataFrame has MultiIndex columns and a top-level key maps to a single column whose remaining sub-level(s) are all "placeholder" values (empty string `""` or NA), pandas has an undocumented convenience behavior that squeezes the result from a 1-column DataFrame into a Series. issues.title: API/BUG: .loc tuple ambiguity with MultiIndex when nlevels == ndim
issues.body_excerpt:
I [the human] asked Claude to post the following:

## Summary

When a DataFrame has a MultiIndex with `nlevels == ndim` (the most common case: a 2-level MI on a 2D DataFrame), tuple keys passed to `.loc` are fundamentally ambiguous between two interpretations:

1. **MI row key**: `df.loc[(a, b)]` means "the row with MultiIndex key `(a, b)`"
2. **Multi-axis indexing**: `df.loc[a, b]` means "row `a`, column `b`"

Python produces the same tuple `(a, b)` for both spellings. The current code resolves this ambiguity differently depending on context — getitem vs setitem, existing vs missing key, scalar vs slice — leading to a cluster of related bugs where the same syntax silently produces different results.

## Related issues

issues.title: PERF: cache BlockManager.get_dtypes() result
issues.body_excerpt:
### Problem

`BaseBlockManager.get_dtypes()` (`pandas/core/internals/managers.py:339`) rebuilds an object array on every call:

```python
def get_dtypes(self) -> npt.NDArray[np.object_]:
    dtypes = np.array([blk.dtype for blk in self.blocks], dtype=object)
    return dtypes.take(self.blknos)
```

It's called from a number of hot paths — `df.dtypes`, `DataFrame.fillna` (`generic.py:6391`), `select_dtypes`/`_get_numeric_data`, `DataFrame.apply` (`frame.py:15751`), `unique_dtypes` in repr/info (`generic.py:7136`), and twice per `iloc` setitem (`indexing.py:944, 975`). For wide, fragmented managers each call is O(nblocks) Python iteration plus an object-array allocation.

issues.title: PERF: skip redundant Index.equals calls in pd.concat
issues.body_excerpt:
### Problem

`pd.concat` compares the same logical pair of indexes twice:

1. `union_indexes` → `all_indexes_same` (`indexes/api.py:337`) walks the inputs pairwise (`first.equals(idx)` for each other), and returns `indexes[0]` when they all match.
2. Then `_get_result` (`reshape/concat.py:652`) re-runs `new_labels.equals(obj_labels)` per obj to decide whether reindexing is needed — re-asking the same question.

In the common case where input frames are separately-constructed with content-equal-but-identity-distinct column indexes, ~50% of all `Index.equals` calls under `pd.concat` are this duplicate.

### Numbers (per call, inputs pre-built outside the timer)

| workload | before | after | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 frames, 50 cols, single-block float | 0.62 ms | 0.50 ms | **1.25x**

issues.title: BUG: Index.get_indexer matches pd.NA against NaN for list input but not ndarray input
issues.body_excerpt:
`Index.get_indexer` gives different answers for `[pd.NA]` (list) vs `np.array([pd.NA], dtype=object)` on a NaN-containing index. This propagates into `Index.drop`, which routes through `com.index_labels_to_array` (producing an ndarray) and so cannot drop a NaN-labeled entry given `pd.NA`.

```python

import pandas as pd

idx = pd.Index([np.nan, "b"])

idx.get_loc(np.nan)                              # 0
idx.get_loc(pd.NA)                               # 0  <- matches

idx.get_indexer([pd.NA])                         # array([0])   <- matches
idx.get_indexer(np.array([pd.NA], dtype=object)) # array([-1])  <- doesn't
idx.get_indexer(pd.Index([pd.NA]))

issues.body_excerpt:
### Problem Description

### Background
While investigating a memory corruption issue yesterday (reported in #65664  and patched in PR #65675 ), I found a structural vulnerability in how the computation engine interacts with Pandas 3.0's Copy-on-Write (CoW) architecture. 

Specifically, `df.eval("new=old", inplace=True)` was bypassing CoW protections. The `eval` engine reached into the `BlockManager`, extracted the raw data arrays, evaluated them, and handed them back. Because the data took a detour through the external computation engine, the CoW reference tracking metadata was stripped. The DataFrame assumed the returned array was unshared memory, leading to silent memory corruption when the alias was later modified.

issues.title: ENH: Support %N directive in strptime parsing (to_datetime / Timestamp with format=)
issues.body_excerpt:
### Problem Description

GH-29461 / PR GH-64899 added a `%N` directive to `Timestamp.strftime` and the
array-level `strftime`, formatting nanoseconds as a 9-digit zero-padded number.
The parsing side does not accept it, so `%N` output doesn't round-trip with the
same format string:

```python
>>> ts = pd.Timestamp("2020-03-14 15:32:52.192548651")
>>> fmt = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%N"
>>> pd.to_datetime(ts.strftime(fmt), format=fmt)
ValueError: 'N' is a bad directive in format '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%N'
```

Note that pandas' strptime already parses nanoseconds via `%f` (it accepts 1-9
digits, an extension over the stdlib's 6), so this is about symmetry and
round-tripping rather than new capability. Suggested in
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/64899#pullrequestreview-4481273478.

issues.title: Potential resource leak when exception occurs during file operation
issues.body_excerpt:
## Bug Report

### Description
When an exception is raised during a file operation, the file handle may not be properly closed, leading to a resource leak.

### Steps to Reproduce
1. Open a file without using a context manager
2. Raise an exception before closing the file
3. The file handle remains open

### Expected Behavior
File handles should always be closed, even when exceptions occur.

### Suggested Fix
Use a `with` statement (context manager) to ensure the file is always closed:

```python
# Instead of:
f = open('file.txt', 'r')
data = f.read()
f.close()

# Use:
with open('file.txt', 'r') as f:
    data = f.read()
```

### Environment
- Python 3.x
- Any OS

This is a common Python pitfall that can cause issues in long-running applications.

issues.body_excerpt:
Ref: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/65807#discussion_r3383822680

```python

The value passed to `__getitem__` on the last line here is `("A", "B")`, which is currently being treated the same way a list would in

issues.title: API: read_sas should decode text by default instead of returning bytes
issues.body_excerpt:
### Problem Description

`read_sas` defaults to `encoding=None`, which returns character columns as object-dtype `bytes`:

```python
>>> pd.read_sas("test1.sas7bdat")["Column2"]
0    b'pear'
dtype: object
```

sas7bdat files record their encoding in the header, so pandas can usually decode without being told. It is also now the only pandas reader that returns bytes by default.

### Feature Description

Deprecate the current default and change it to `encoding="infer"`, which decodes using the header-declared encoding (falling back to `latin-1` when the code is unrecognized). For XPORT, which has no encoding field, `"infer"` means `ISO-8859-1` — matching `XportReader`'s own default, which `read_sas` currently overrides with `None`.

`encoding=None` stays available for users who want raw byte

The Installation guide instructs users to activate a conda environment using legacy syntax:

activate name_of_my_env

`source activate` / `activate` was conda's activation syntax before conda 4.4 (released in 2017), and has since been replaced by `conda activate` which works across all operating systems (e.g. Windows, MacOS, Linux).

issues.title: BUG: datetimelike arithmetic landing on the NaT sentinel silently returns NaT
issues.body_excerpt:
### Summary

`NaT` is stored as `INT64_MIN`, so any datetimelike arithmetic whose result lands exactly on
`INT64_MIN` is indistinguishable from a missing value once stored. `@cython.overflowcheck(True)`
catches a sum that goes *below* `INT64_MIN` but not one that lands *on* it, so there is a
one-step hole at the bottom of the range: the step further out raises, the step onto the
sentinel silently returns `NaT`.

GH-66510 / GH-66520 closed this for parsing and construction. It is still open across
arithmetic, and it is not a single site — it recurs everywhere pandas does datetimelike
addition, and in a few places as a bare `assert` rather than a silent `NaT`.

issues.title: BUG: segfault on next() after a chunked read_csv chunk raised (C engine)
issues.body_excerpt:
### Reproducible Example

```python
import io

import pandas as pd

# column "b" has one non-numeric token, so converting the first chunk raises
data = "a,b\n" + "".join(f"{i},{'oops' if i == 5 else i}\n" for i in range(20))

reader = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(data), dtype={"b": "int64"}, chunksize=10)

try:
    next(reader)
except ValueError:
    pass  # invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'oops'

next(reader)  # <-- segfault
```

### Issue Description

If converting a chunk raises, the `TextFileReader` is left in a state where the
next `next()` / `get_chunk()` call segfaults instead of raising.

No pyarrow, no datetimes — just int values against string categories, and vice versa:

```python

# 0    NaN
# 1    NaN
# dtype: category
# Categories (2, str): ['1', '2']

# the two-step cast, which is what was meant:
pd.Categorical(pd.Series([1, 2]).astype("str"),
               dtype=pd.C

issues.body_excerpt:
Discussed in Dev Meeting 8/12/26.  Inspired by https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas-stubs/issues/1876

For various methods/constructors in `pandas`, we indicate that the arguments should be "array-like".  This includes `list`, `Sequence` (but not strings), numpy arrays.  In some cases at runtime, we also allow other iterables (e.g., dicts, generators), and disallow some iterables (e.g., sets), although this is not completely documented.

pd.Index({"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3}) # Uses keys as

issues.title: PERF: avoid per-element group labels in nullable DataFrame axis=1 reductions
issues.body_excerpt:
### Reproducible Example

The existing `axis=1` reduction path for homogeneous ExtensionArray-backed DataFrames concatenates the columns into a one-dimensional array. It then constructs the row labels with:

```python
row_index = np.tile(np.arange(nrows), ncols)
```

This creates one group label for every element in the DataFrame. The flattened values and labels are subsequently passed to `_groupby_op` with `ngroups=nrows`.

For supported nullable masked and Arrow numeric or Boolean arrays, the existing groupby kernels can instead operate on column-major data and mask buffers viewed as `(nrows, ncols)`. The specialized path requires only `ncols` zero-valued group IDs and one group. This retains the kernel and the ordering of columns within each row while avoiding the `nrows * ncols` label

issues.title: ENH: Add optional checkpointing and recovery for long-running apply operations
issues.body_excerpt:
### Problem Description

Long-running Series.apply() and DataFrame.apply() operations can be vulnerable to unexpected process or kernel termination.

Currently, intermediate results are kept in memory until the operation completes. If the Python process terminates unexpectedly, all successfully computed intermediate results may be lost, even if most or all rows have already been processed.

It would be useful to provide an optional checkpointing mechanism that periodically persists completed results during apply() execution.

For example, users could specify a checkpoint file and checkpoint interval. If execution is interrupted, a subsequent run could restore the checkpoint and continue processing only the remaining rows.

This could be particularly useful for expensive per-row operations

issues.title: API: Replace `na_action` with `skipna` in map methods
issues.body_excerpt:
Split out from #61128

The map methods currently take `na_action: Literal["ignore"] | None = None`:

- Series.map
- DataFrame.map
- Index.map
- CategoricalIndex.map
- ExtensionArray.map and its subclasses (Categorical, datetimelike, SparseArray, Arrow, masked)
- pandas.core.algorithms.map_array

On reading code, it seems hard to me to guess what both `na_action=None` and `na_action="ignore"` do. Better I think would be `skipna`:

```python
# current
ser.map(func, na_action=None)
ser.map(func, na_action="ignore")

# proposed
ser.map(func, skipna=False)
ser.map(func, skipna=True)         
```

Proposal

1. Add `skipna` to the methods above. The default keeps current behavior.
2. Deprecate `na_action`. Passing both na_action and skipna raises.
3. Remove `na_action` in the next major release.

issues.title: ENH: NDFrame.ax accessor for Index method pass-through
issues.body_excerpt:
Reviving a variant of #52461.

A common operation is

```
df = df.copy(deep=False)
df.index = df.index.some_method()
```

We already have some NDFrame methods that inline this to return the new `df`: tz_localize, tz_convert, to_period, to_timestamp, swaplevel, reorder_levels, droplevel, rename_axis.  #34254 is a request to add `to_flat_index` to this list.

I propose a new accessor, name TBD, placeholder `ax` to pass through *any* index-transforming (length-retaining) method.  So the above could example becomes:

```
df = df.ax.some_method()
df = df.ax.some_method(axis=1)  # to do the same for columns
```

In #52461 I advocated deprecating the names already on NDFrame in favor of the new version.  I am no longer advocating that, but would be open to it.
